title: Case study: notification system
objective: Design a notification system: respect each user's settings, give each channel its own queue, stay under providers' rate limits, and retry without sending twice.

sources.title: Firebase docs: FCM throttling and quotas (Android: up to 240 messages a minute and 5,000 an hour to one device; over quota returns 429)
IETF RFC 6585: HTTP status code 429 Too Many Requests
AWS documentation: Amazon SQS dead-letter queues
Stripe: Designing robust and predictable APIs with idempotency

simplifies: A generic design, not any one company's. Real systems add templates in many languages, delivery tracking, in-app inboxes, and legal rules about marketing messages. The FCM limits are from its docs; other numbers are illustrative.

steps.caption: Requirements: many services (orders, chat, marketing) send notifications by push, email and SMS. Users choose what they get. Important ones must not be lost; nobody should get the same one twice.
One notifier: services send "this event happened for this user", not "send this SMS". Channel details, templates and rules live in one place.
Settings first: the notifier checks what the user agreed to (marketing off, quiet hours at night) before anything is queued.

predict.prompt: A user turned off marketing notifications. Two events arrive: "your order has shipped" and "weekend sale starts now". What gets sent?

options.explanation: Right. It's about their own order; the sale is marketing, which they turned off.

options.text: Both: the system can't tell them apart
options.explanation: Each event has a type, and that's what the setting checks.

steps.caption: Each channel has its own queue and workers. A slow SMS provider then only delays SMS; push and email keep flowing.

predict.prompt: Why give each channel its own queue instead of one shared queue?

options.text: So a slow or failing channel can't hold up the others
options.explanation: Right. It's isolation: one provider's trouble stays in its own lane.

options.text: Because queues can only hold one kind of message
options.explanation: A queue can hold anything; the reason is isolation.

options.text: To send each notification on every channel
options.explanation: Which channels to use is a settings decision, not a queue one.

steps.caption: Rate limits: providers cap how fast you may send. Firebase Cloud Messaging documents up to 240 messages a minute and 5,000 an hour to one Android device, and answers 429 over quota. Workers send at a steady rate and back off on 429.

Retries: a provider times out, so the worker tries again later. Each notification has its own ID, so the retry can't produce a second copy. One that keeps failing goes to a dead-letter queue; an invalid device token is removed, not retried forever.

Failure: the SMS provider is down for 20 minutes. Its queue grows while push and email carry on. A login code that is 20 minutes old is useless, so time-sensitive notifications have an expiry and are dropped instead of sent late.

critique.prompt: A proposal: every service calls the push, email and SMS providers directly; nobody checks user settings; when a provider call fails, the service retries at once, in a loop, until it works.

risks.text: Retrying at once in a loop hammers a provider that's already struggling, and hits its rate limit for everyone
risks.why: Back off between retries, cap the number of tries, and park failures in a dead-letter queue.

risks.text: No settings check: users get marketing they turned off
risks.why: Check settings in one place before anything is sent.

risks.text: Each service has its own copy of the sending logic, so limits and fixes must be repeated everywhere
risks.why: One notifier owns channels, limits and retries.

risks.text: Notifications are sent after the order is saved, not while the customer waits
risks.why: That's right: sending in the background keeps checkout fast.

risks.text: Email and push use different templates
risks.why: They're different formats; separate templates are normal.

critique.hint: Think about a provider having a bad minute, a user who said no to marketing, and who has to fix things when a limit changes.

first.prompt: During a big sale, the push provider starts answering 429, and soon no push notifications go out at all, not even order updates. Which fix comes first?

options.text: Back off on 429 and limit the sending rate
options.explanation: Right. Tight retry loops keep the quota exhausted; backing off lets important notifications through.
Needed, but it doesn't stop the retry storm.

options.text: Move the sending logic into one notifier
options.explanation: That's where the fix should live, but the urgent part is backing off.

critique.explain: Fix what's stopping everything first: retry storms keep the provider's limit exhausted. Then centralise sending in one notifier with a settings check, so limits and rules live in one place.

quiz.prompt: A worker's request to the push provider times out. Why is it safe to retry?

options.text: The notification has its own ID, so a retry that reaches the provider twice is still only delivered once
options.explanation: Right. Same idea as idempotency keys in payments.

options.text: Timeouts mean the request definitely failed
options.explanation: A timeout means you don't know; it may have gone through.

options.text: It isn't safe: never retry notifications
options.explanation: Without retries, a brief blip loses notifications.

quiz.prompt: Why do login codes get an expiry time in the queue?

options.text: A code that arrives after it has stopped working is useless, so it's better dropped than sent late
options.explanation: Right. Time-sensitive notifications lose their value quickly.
The reason is usefulness, not storage.
Providers send what they're given; the notifier must decide.
